blocks.body: Planners commonly advise a cooling-off period — a few months in an insured savings account or Treasury bills — before large decisions. Its purpose is behavioral: sudden money invites rushed purchases and pressure from others. Deposit insurance covers {{fig:fdic_standard_max_deposit}} per depositor, per bank, for each ownership category, so spread a larger sum across banks or hold Treasury bills. Three things cannot wait for the cooling-off period. If anyone in the household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, a lump sum can end eligibility (SSI's resource limit is {{fig:ssi_resource_limit_individual}} for an individual), so report it and ask before moving the money; an ABLE account or a special-needs trust can sometimes keep a person with a disability eligible. Taxable windfalls — lottery or gambling wins, back pay, most legal settlements other than for physical injury or sickness — are income for the year, so set the tax aside; if too little was withheld, an estimated tax payment can help avoid an underpayment penalty. And a decision to disclaim an inheritance must generally be made in writing within 9 months and before you accept the asset; using it or directing what happens to it can count as accepting.
blocks.plain: Financial planners often suggest waiting a few months — with the money in an insured savings account or Treasury bills — before making big decisions. The point is about behavior: sudden money invites rushed purchases and pressure from other people. Deposit insurance covers {{fig:fdic_standard_max_deposit}} for each depositor at each bank, for each type of account ownership, so split a larger amount across banks or buy Treasury bills. Three things can't wait for that pause. If anyone in your household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or housing help, a lump sum can end that help (SSI's limit on what you can own is {{fig:ssi_resource_limit_individual}} for one person), so report it and ask before you move the money; an ABLE account or a special-needs trust can sometimes keep a person with a disability eligible. Windfalls that are taxable — lottery or gambling wins, back pay, most legal settlements that are not for a physical injury or sickness — count as income for the year, so set the tax money aside; if not enough tax was withheld, paying estimated tax can help you avoid a penalty. And if you inherited the money and might turn it down (a "disclaimer"), you generally must do that in writing within 9 months and before you accept it; using the money or telling others what to do with it can count as accepting.

blocks.body: Cash, a brokerage account, an inherited IRA and a house are taxed differently. Inherited assets generally get a basis stepped up to value at the date of death, so selling soon after inheriting often produces little gain. Most non-spouse beneficiaries of an inherited IRA must empty it within 10 years, and if the original owner had started required distributions, annual distributions are required during those years too. A non-spouse beneficiary cannot roll an inherited IRA into their own; move it only by direct trustee-to-trustee transfer into an account titled as inherited, because a check made out to you counts as a withdrawal and cannot be put back.
blocks.plain: Cash, a brokerage account, an inherited IRA and a house are taxed in different ways. Inherited things usually get a new cost basis equal to their value on the day of death (a "step-up"), so selling soon after you inherit often creates little taxable gain. Most people who inherit an IRA from someone other than a spouse must empty it within 10 years. If the original owner had already started required withdrawals, you must also take yearly withdrawals during those years. If you inherit an IRA from someone other than a spouse, you can't roll it into your own IRA. Move it only by a direct transfer from one company to the other, into an account labeled as inherited; a check made out to you counts as a withdrawal and can't be put back.

blocks.body: Vanguard's historical study found that investing a lump sum immediately beat spreading it out over time in about two-thirds of rolling periods, because markets rise more often than they fall. Spreading it out buys protection against regret if the market drops soon after. Both are defensible; pick the one you will stick with.
blocks.plain: Vanguard looked at past market history and found that investing a lump sum right away beat spreading it out over time in about two-thirds of the periods it studied, because markets go up more often than they go down. Spreading it out protects you from regret if the market falls right after you invest. Both are reasonable; choose the one you'll stick with.
